summary: This Standards Track document defines how to send ordinary DNS queries (OPCODE 0) over the Constrained Application Protocol. The messages can be protected with (D)TLS-secured CoAP or OSCORE, giving encrypted DNS for constrained Internet of Things devices.

eli5.summary: Tiny gadgets also need to look up internet names. This lets them ask in a short, lightweight, private way.

questions: how does doc differ from doh
subtitle: How tiny Internet of Things devices can look up names by carrying DNS messages inside CoAP.

tldr.problem: Constrained IoT devices have little memory, small link-layer frames and slow links, so DNS over HTTPS or DNS over DTLS is a poor fit for them.
tldr.mechanism: DNS over CoAP (DoC) sends each DNS query in the body of a CoAP FETCH request and returns the DNS response in the CoAP response, protected by (D)TLS or OSCORE.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that gives constrained devices encrypted DNS and lets CoAP proxies cache answers.

today: RFC 9953 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs a CoAP Version
sections.content:
RFC 9953 defines DNS over CoAP (DoC). It sends DNS queries and gets DNS responses over the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) using OPCODE 0 (Query). Each DNS query-response pair is mapped onto one CoAP message exchange.

The use case is inspired by DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), but HTTPS often conflicts with constrained devices. Such devices may have only a handful of kilobytes of RAM and ROM, link-layer frames of a few hundred bytes, bit rates of kilobits per second and latencies of several seconds. DNS over DTLS (RFC 8094) avoids TCP and HTTPS, but DoC can use CoAP features instead: block-wise transfer, CoAP proxies that add a caching level, and reuse of data structures for application traffic and DNS information.

To avoid the cost of DTLS or TLS, DoC also allows lightweight message protection with OSCORE.
sections.eli5: Small devices cannot carry heavy luggage. DNS over CoAP is a light backpack for carrying a name lookup, instead of a big suitcase.

sections.title: Finding a DoC Server
sections.content:
A DoC server acts as a DNS stub or recursive resolver, and a DoC resource is the CoAP resource a client targets. No path is specified for it, but the root path / is RECOMMENDED to keep requests small. The client can learn the server by manual configuration of a URI, or automatically through a CoRE resource directory, DHCP or Router Advertisement options, or discovery of designated resolvers. Automatic configuration MUST only be done from a trusted source.

For link-based discovery, the RFC introduces the resource type core.dns to identify a generic DNS resolver.

A server can also be found through SVCB records or DNR. The RFC defines a single-valued, mandatory SvcParamKey called docpath for DoC. Its value lists the segments of the absolute path to the DoC resource, each 1 to 255 octets, and the root path is the empty list. The client builds a request from the record: alpn=coap means CoAP over TLS, alpn=co means CoAP over DTLS, the port comes from the port SvcParam or defaults to 5684, and each docpath element becomes a Uri-Path option. If the request gets a response, the same record is reused for later queries; otherwise the client falls back to the record with the next priority.

Servers that support only OSCORE and EDHOC for security cannot be discovered with SVCB or DNR. The RFC leaves another discovery mechanism out of scope.
sections.eli5: Before you can ask a question you need to know who to ask and where they live. A device can be told, or it can look the address up in a directory.

sections.title: DNS Queries in CoAP Requests
sections.content:
A DoC client encodes a single DNS query in one or more CoAP request messages that use the CoAP FETCH method (RFC 8132). The DNS query goes in the request body, and the Content-Format option MUST say what it is. The RFC defines the Content-Format ID 553 for application/dns-message, a single DNS message in the DNS wire format. Requests SHOULD include an Accept option.

Using FETCH puts the query in the body, as POST does in DoH, while keeping the caching advantages of GET. There is no need for base64 encoding, and queries can be sent block-wise. Because CoAP provides reliability at the message layer, the DNS retransmission mechanism is not needed.

To let CoAP caches such as proxies answer repeated queries, the client SHOULD set the DNS header ID to 0, so the CoAP cache key does not change between identical queries. The server MUST copy the ID from the query into its response.

Only OPCODE 0 is specified. For a query with an OPCODE the server does not implement, the server uses RCODE 4 (NotImp).
sections.eli5: The device writes its question on a note and hands it over with a label saying what kind of note it is. Using the same blank question number each time lets helpers remember the answer.

sections.title: Responses, Errors and Caching
sections.content:
The DNS response travels in the body of the CoAP response, also with the option of block-wise transfer. A DoC server MUST be able to produce application/dns-message responses, and every client MUST be able to parse them. CoAP responses that carry a parsable DNS response are RECOMMENDED to use code 2.05 (Content).

Errors are split by layer. Problems talking to an upstream DNS server, such as timeouts, MUST be reported as a DNS response with the right RCODE inside a successful 2.xx CoAP response. CoAP error codes MUST NOT carry a DNS response and are for CoAP-layer errors or requests that break the DoC rules, for example 4.15 (Unsupported Content-Format).

For caching, the server MUST make sure the sum of the CoAP Max-Age and any TTL in the DNS response is less than or equal to the TTL it received upstream. The client MUST add the Max-Age to all TTLs on reception. The RECOMMENDED server algorithm sets Max-Age to the minimum TTL of the response and subtracts that value from all TTLs, which also keeps an ETag based on content stable. For errors or answers without TTLs, Max-Age SHOULD be set to a suitable shorter period.
sections.eli5: If the phone book is closed, the answer still comes back saying so. Only if the post office itself breaks do you get a post office error. Answers also carry a best-before time so helpers know how long to remember them.

sections.title: Observe, OSCORE and Other CoAP Features
sections.content:
DNS Push Notifications add overhead that conflicts with constrained resources, so the RFC RECOMMENDS using CoAP Observe instead in the DoC domain. A DoC server SHOULD offer Observe on its DoC resource and keeps a list of observers. It MAY subscribe to DNS Push for the record upstream, and SHOULD cancel the subscription once no observers remain. When a push arrives for an observed record, the server sends an Observe notification to the client.

It is RECOMMENDED to carry DNS messages protected with OSCORE between the client and server. Setting up and maintaining the OSCORE security context is out of scope.

The RFC gives no mapping between DoC and DoH, for example at a CoAP-to-HTTP proxy, and such a direct mapping is NOT RECOMMENDED because rewriting FETCH and TTLs would be non-trivial. A DNS forwarder is the recommended way to bridge the two.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking again and again whether the answer changed, the device can ask to be told when it changes. Letters can also be put in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Security and Unprotected Use
sections.content:
Using DoC without confidentiality and integrity protection is NOT RECOMMENDED. Setting the DNS ID to 0 opens a client's cache to response spoofing when CoAP is unprotected, so an unprotected DoC message MUST use a random token of at least 2 bytes to guard against off-path poisoning. With (D)TLS or OSCORE an unpredictable ID is unnecessary, so the ID can stay 0 to benefit from caching.

DoC only protects the hop between parties that share a security context. The server may talk to the upstream DNS infrastructure unprotected, for example over DNS over UDP, and the client cannot see that. A client that cannot do DNSSEC validation, for instance because of code size, may trust its DoC server to do it. How that trust is expressed is out of scope.

DoC also inherits the security considerations of CoAP, OSCORE and DTLS. The RFC notes that many CoAP implementations still use DTLS 1.2, so it accounts for it while recommending newer versions.
sections.eli5: Passing notes in the open lets a sneaky classmate swap them. Sealed envelopes stop that, so open notes need a secret random number to prove they are real.

sections.title: Running DoC in a Network
sections.content:
Many DNS transports can coexist on a DoC server, such as UDP, (D)TLS, HTTPS and QUIC. Transports with channel or object security should in principle be preferred, and in constrained scenarios DoC is preferable to DNS over DTLS, though the final choice is left to implementers and users. The RFC does not enforce Confirmable or Non-Confirmable CoAP messages.

CoAP does not support redirection at the time of writing. The Hop-Limit option can mitigate infinite loops among CoAP proxies. If a client gets no successful DNS messages from its server for a while, it should treat that like a recursive resolver that lost upstream connectivity. Transport-specific DNS extensions, such as the edns-tcp-keepalive option, do not apply to DoC.

IANA assigned Content-Format 553, registered SvcParamKey number 10 named docpath, and added the resource type core.dns.
sections.eli5: A helper can answer questions in many ways, like by phone or letter. The RFC does not say which to pick, but says the safe, small way is good for tiny devices.
